pi.name: Ariangela J. Kozik
pi.title: Assistant Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: Ariangela J. Kozik earned a B.S. in Biotechnology from Calvin College and a Ph.D. in Comparative Pathobiology from Purdue University, followed by training in Personalized and Genomic Medicine at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus. She was an NIH-fellowship-supported postdoctoral fellow studying the respiratory microbiome and asthma and then a Research Investigator in pulmonary medicine at Michigan Medicine, focusing on microbial-immune relationships in adult asthma with an emphasis on precision approaches. She is now an Assistant Professor in MCDB with affiliations in Internal Medicine (Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine), the Center for Computational Medicine and Bioinformatics, and AI and Digital Health Innovation. She co-founded the Black Microbiologists Association in 2020.

description: The Kozik Lab investigates host-microbe and microbe-microbe crosstalk in the human respiratory tract, with a focus on how immune-microbiome interactions shape chronic respiratory disease, particularly asthma. The lab uses multi-omic approaches spanning the microbiome, genome, transcriptome, metabolome, and proteome to understand dynamic interactions in the airways and asthma heterogeneity. A major experimental focus is the genus Prevotella, including how the lung symbiont Prevotella melaninogenica tolerates oxygen, how it can be made genetically and experimentally tractable, and whether lung commensals metabolize inhaled corticosteroids. The lab also works to advance precision medicine by measuring lived environmental conditions rather than relying on broad population labels. Its stated values are teamwork, communication, curiosity, and community, with a commitment that science belongs to everyone.

areas.title: The Prevotella paradox and oxygen adaptation
areas.summary: Asks how Prevotella melaninogenica, classified as a strict anaerobe for over a century, thrives in the oxygenated respiratory tract. The lab's preprinted work shows active growth in hypoxic conditions and gene expression shifts suggesting oxygen tolerance, and it is identifying mechanisms of oxygen detection and neutralization and their effects on microbe-microbe competition and persistence during airway inflammation.

areas.title: Expanding experimental tractability for Prevotella
areas.summary: Develops laboratory protocols and genetic tools so that Prevotella can be studied functionally in controlled settings, moving beyond observational genomic correlations.

areas.title: Microbial biotransformation of inhaled corticosteroids
areas.summary: Explores whether lung commensals, especially Prevotella species, carry biochemical machinery that metabolically alters inhaled corticosteroids, potentially explaining partial or complete nonresponsiveness in some patients.

areas.title: The ecosocial interface
areas.summary: Works to advance precision medicine in microbiome research by shifting from broad population labels toward direct measurement of the lived environmental conditions that influence health outcomes.
